english: Then the number of integers $n$ with $1\le n\le 100$ for which $D_n$ is the square of an integer is
hindi: प्रत्येक धनात्मक पूर्णांक $n$ के लिए माना कि
है। तब $1\le n\le 100$ वाले उन पूर्णांकों $n$ की संख्या, जिनके लिए $D_n$ किसी पूर्णांक का वर्ग है,
solution: $D_n=9(n+1)$, a perfect square $\iff n+1$ is a perfect square
solution_full: The matrix is circulant: each row is the previous one shifted cyclically, so every row and every column has sum $3n+3$.
Apply $C_1\to C_1+C_2+C_3$; the first column becomes $(3n+3,3n+3,3n+3)$, and $3(n+1)$ comes out as a common factor.
So $D_n=9(n+1)$. This agrees with the circulant formula $a^{3}+b^{3}+c^{3}-3abc=(a+b+c)\cdot\frac12[(a-b)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}+(c-a)^{2}]=(3n+3)\cdot3$.
Since $9$ is a square, $D_n$ is a perfect square exactly when $n+1$ is a perfect square.
For $1\le n\le 100$ we have $2\le n+1\le 101$, and the squares in this range are $4,9,\dots,100$, that is $k^{2}$ for $k=2,\dots,10$.
Hence $9$ values of $n$ (namely $n=3,8,15,\dots,99$). Including $n+1=1$ (outside the range) would give $10$.
originality_note: New: a circulant determinant with consecutive entries collapses to 9(n+1), turning the question into counting perfect squares in a range (way 5). Closest known: proving the circulant identity a^3+b^3+c^3-3abc as a factorisation. Different because: the factorisation is only the first step; the question is arithmetic on the resulting expression.
blueprint_concepts: Special forms: circulant and Vandermonde determinants

concept_use.Special forms: circulant and Vandermonde: The circulant structure (equal row sums, factor a+b+c and the second factor 1/2 sum of squared differences) gives D_n = 9(n+1).
concept_use.Application of properties of determinant: C1 -> C1+C2+C3, taking out the common factor 3(n+1), and R2-R1, R3-R1 are the properties used.
